refuter_findings.location: ## Definition, Fourier coefficients: the L1 real-valuedness equivalence
refuter_findings.evidence: The deps list includes thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus but not thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp. The Definition relies on Fejer convergence at p=1 for the reverse implication. The listed Fourier-basis theorem establishes the coefficient isometry and Parseval for L2, which does not license the L1 Fourier uniqueness used to conclude that the field is real almost everywhere.

The Definition refers to a scalar field in 'the analogous scalar spaces,' but its coefficient families, norms, and H^s definition specify only C3-valued fields. The pressure item then asserts that a real scalar field p belongs to H^m; the scalar spaces have not been defined.

The Statement assumes a<b and defines the integral only on positive-length intervals, but claim 2 sets G(a)=integral_a^a and claim 3 allows c=a or c=b. Step 4.1 uses zero-length subintegrals, and step 5.1 invokes negative increments without an oriented-integral convention. These expressions are undefined as stated.

The displayed estimate ends with an expression containing an unbound m and the word 'summed'; it is not a well-formed inequality. The following 'more explicitly' finite-partial-sum estimate supplies the intended bound, so the malformed display does not obstruct the proof.

F1 justifies the weighted l1 estimate by the pointwise inequality (2π|k|∞)^|α|≤w_k^|α|≤w_k^(2σ'). A pointwise bound does not establish summability. The lattice-sum dependency plus weighted Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the estimate, but that argument is absent.

Step 2.2 uses B(x0,δ) in T3. Its metric-ball dependency defines balls for a metric space (X,d), while this item and its topology dependencies give T3 a quotient/product topology without specifying a metric on it.
Step 3.1 invokes the fundamental theorem of calculus on a torus segment for each finite Fourier sum. No FTC supplier is in the item's deps, and the step does not derive the identity locally.

The input u is an H^sigma equivalence class, but claim 3 says 'u is in C^j'. Claim 1 constructs the canonical representative tilde u, and the displayed derivatives are those of tilde u; state that this representative has the regularity.

refuter_findings.location: ## Statement, claim 2 and Facts & Assumptions, F5
refuter_findings.evidence: The Statement fixes H^sigma as vector fields into R3, then uses the pointwise product fg and coefficient products of vector-valued Fourier coefficients without defining a multiplication or output type. Step 4.1 also applies claim 2 to a scalar component f_j and a vector field, outside claim 2's stated domain.

Step 1.1 proves the identity for divergence-free polynomial u, then uses F4's density of all trigonometric polynomials to extend it to every divergence-free u; F4 does not supply density within the divergence-free subspace. Step 2.1 names u_N=P_Nu as 'the Fourier truncation' but gives no cutoff definition or listed dependency for P_N, so the needed divergence-preserving approximation is not established.

F6 uses u tensor u and div(u tensor u), but the cited definition defines divergence only for vector fields and no listed dependency defines a tensor product or matrix divergence. Step 2.1 uses this undefined expression to show the mean vanishes.

Step 1.1 establishes that X_N is spanned by finitely many vectors, then step 4.1 fixes an ordered basis. The cited basis item explicitly says its definition does not assert basis existence, and the coordinate-map theorem assumes an ordered basis. No finite spanning-set-to-basis argument is supplied.

F2 asserts H^p×H^p to H^(p−1) for the transport map for every p>3/2. The cited product result gives H^sigma×H^(sigma+1) to H^sigma for sigma>3/2, which directly yields the stated form only for p>5/2. The proof can use sufficiently high orders, but this broader fact is not established.

Step 2.1 passes from the H^p-valued derivative u'=G to a pointwise time derivative and joint C^1 regularity without applying point evaluation as a bounded linear functional. The embedding dependency supplies the required bound, but the argument does not make this step.
The title asserts T=(2C_sY_0)^−1 without a condition. The Statement defines T=1 when Y_0=0, where the title's quotient is undefined.

The title says the higher norms stay bounded uniformly in N, but the Statement assumes only u_0 in H^s and explicitly assigns B_m=∞ when a higher initial norm is infinite. For example, real-symmetric coefficients u_hat(±(2^n,0,0))=w_(2^n,0,0)^(-s)e_2/n define a divergence-free u_0 in H^s but not H^(s+1); the H^(s+1) norms of its Fourier truncations at t=0 grow without bound.

Step 3.1 asserts the integral identity for every t in [0,T], including t=0. Its cited integral supplier defines the integral only when the interval has positive length and does not define integral_0^0.

The equation has been established only at Sobolev orders m≥s, but step 4.1 says to take an integer m≥p for arbitrary p. That choice need not satisfy m≥s; choose m≥max(s,p) when using the proved equation.
Claim 1 asserts that the real scalar pressure p belongs to H^m for every m, but the cited definition defines H^m for R3-valued fields and only names undefined 'analogous scalar spaces'.
F3 states the product estimate without restricting m, while the cited product result requires sigma>3/2. The proof later uses the estimate only for r>3/2, but F3 as written has broader scope.

Step 3.1 concludes that q−p is zero everywhere from all Fourier coefficients being zero, then cites only the embedding result that continuous fields equal almost everywhere are equal everywhere. Fourier coefficient injectivity/Parseval is needed to obtain equality almost everywhere and is not stated in the proof.

reader_findings.location: ## Definition, Fourier coefficients: the L1 real-valuedness equivalence
reader_findings.evidence: The reverse implication relies on L1 Fourier uniqueness and cites thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp, but that supplier is absent from this item's deps. The included Fourier-basis theorem is stated for L2 and does not supply general L1 uniqueness.

reader_findings.location: ## Definition, operators: “a scalar field f ... in the analogous scalar spaces”
reader_findings.evidence: The item defines H^s(T^3;R^3), but only names “analogous scalar spaces” without defining their coefficient families, norms, or scalar H^s notation. The pressure item then asserts p belongs to H^m as a scalar field.

reader_findings.location: ## Statement, claims 2–3; ## Proof, steps 4.1 and 5.1
reader_findings.evidence: The integral is introduced only for a<b, but G(a)=integral_a^a g is required, claim 3 allows c=a or c=b, and step 4.1 uses zero-length subintegrals. Step 5.1 also invokes the same argument for negative increments without an oriented-integral convention. Define these cases or rewrite the uses.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 3.1
reader_findings.evidence: The displayed comparison ends with a right-hand expression containing an unbound m and the word “summed”; it is not a well-formed inequality. The subsequent “more explicitly” sentence gives the intended finite-partial-sum estimate, but the preceding computation should be replaced.

reader_findings.location: ## Facts & Assumptions, F1
reader_findings.evidence: The asserted multi-index weighted l1 estimate is justified only by (2π|k|∞)^|α|≤w_k^|α|≤w_k^(2σ'). A pointwise bound by w_k^(2σ') does not establish summability. The cited lattice lemma's general weight-sum claim plus weighted Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the estimate, but that argument is absent.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 2.2
reader_findings.evidence: The proof uses a metric ball B(x0,delta) in T^3, but the declared structure is the quotient/product topology and no metric on T^3 is defined by the item or its dependencies. Use an open neighborhood or specify a metric.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 3.1
reader_findings.evidence: The termwise-differentiation argument invokes the fundamental theorem of calculus on a torus segment for each finite Fourier sum. No FTC supplier is in deps and no local derivation is given.

reader_findings.location: ## Statement, claim 3
reader_findings.evidence: The input u is an H^sigma equivalence class, while C^j is a class of pointwise fields. Claim 1 constructs the unique representative tilde u, but claim 3 says “u is in C^j”; state that the canonical representative tilde u has this regularity.

reader_findings.location: ## Statement, claim 2 and Facts & Assumptions F5
reader_findings.evidence: The item fixes H^sigma as vector fields into R^3, then writes fg and the coefficient product hat f(l) hat g(k-l) without defining a vector multiplication or output type. Specify scalar inputs or define the intended componentwise/tensor product.

reader_findings.location: ## Facts & Assumptions, F6; ## Proof, step 2.1
reader_findings.evidence: F6 uses u tensor u and div(u tensor u), but the dependencies define divergence only for vector fields and do not define a tensor product or matrix divergence. Define those operations or give the componentwise product-rule identity used to show the mean is zero.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, steps 1.1 and 4.1
reader_findings.evidence: The proof establishes that X_N is spanned by finitely many vectors and then fixes an ordered basis, but cites no finite spanning-set-to-basis result and supplies no elimination argument.

reader_findings.location: ## Facts & Assumptions, F2
reader_findings.evidence: The cited product supplier gives H^sigma×H^sigma→H^sigma and H^sigma×H^(sigma+1)→H^sigma for sigma>3/2. It does not state the claimed transport map H^p×H^p→H^(p−1) for every p>3/2. The proof can use sufficiently high orders, but this broader fact needs proof or a narrower hypothesis.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 2.1
reader_findings.evidence: An H^p-valued derivative u'=G does not identify the pointwise time derivative until evaluation at x is applied as a bounded linear functional. The embedding gives that bound, but the proof does not make this step when concluding joint C^1 regularity.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 3.1
reader_findings.evidence: The integral identity is asserted for t in [0,T], including t=0, but the cited Riemann-curve integral supplier only defines the integral for positive interval length and does not define integral_0^0. Handle t=0 separately or state the convention.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 4.1
reader_findings.evidence: The equation has been established for Sobolev orders m>=s, but this paragraph says to take an integer m>=p for arbitrary p. Choose m>=max(s,p); the stated choice alone does not ensure the proved equation is available.

reader_findings.location: ## Statement, claim 1
reader_findings.evidence: p is a real scalar field, but H^m in the cited definition is defined for R^3-valued fields; the supplier only mentions undefined “analogous scalar spaces.” State or define scalar Sobolev spaces before asserting p belongs to H^m.

reader_findings.location: ## Facts & Assumptions, F3
reader_findings.evidence: The product estimate supplied by lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product requires m>3/2, but F3 states it without that restriction. The proof later uses bounds at r>3/2, so the fact should state its scope.

reader_findings.location: ## Proof, step 3.1
reader_findings.evidence: Equal Fourier coefficients imply q−p=0 almost everywhere by Fourier coefficient injectivity/Parseval, but the cited embedding claim 2 only says continuous fields equal almost everywhere are equal everywhere. The proof omits the coefficient-injectivity step needed before applying that claim.
